newsitem.title: TURKEY: Pressure mounts on Turkish Islamist Erbakan.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Turkish Islamist Erbakan.

text.p: Turkey's secularist majority joined ranks with the pro-Western army on Monday in an assault on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist ambitions.
Several thousand anti-Islamist demonstrators took to the streets of Istanbul and a veteran politician warned Erbakan to respect democracy and toe the official secularist line.
"I told him that if he can't do that then he should leave the government," former prime minister Bulent Ecevit told a news conference after meeting Erbakan.
A recent increase in army criticism of the coalition has stirred memories of three previous military coups since 1960.
But Erbakan brushed off the generals' latest efforts to influence the running of the country.
"In Turkey governments are formed in parliament, not in the National Security Council (NSC). Laws are made in parliament," he told a news conference.
The military-dominated council warned Erbakan at the weekend to end a recent surge in religious activism they fear could pave the way to turning NATO member Turkey into an Islamist state.
The Yeni Yuzyil daily quoted a prominent member of Erbakan's Welfare Party on Monday as calling for the government to heed the military warning.
"Welfare should take steps to smooth this out," the paper quoted MP Aydin Menderes as saying.
Erbakan, 70, became modern Turkey's first Islamist leader last year in alliance with conservatives after narrowly winning general elections with 21 percent of the vote.
Many secularists say he does not have a mandate to raise the profile of Islam in public life.

Several thousand people, mostly women, sang republican marching songs and chanted anti-government slogans in Istanbul's central Taksim Square at a ceremony to mark the anniversary of a key date in Turkey's secularist calendar.

Military leader Kemal Ataturk scrapped the 1,300-year-old caliphate of Sunni Islam on March 3, 1924 as part of wideranging Westernising reforms. The caliphate had last been held by the Turkish Ottoman sultans overthrown by Ataturk.
"Turkey is secular and will stay secular," protesters sang. Others laid flowers at a statue of Ataturk, witnesses said.
Today's generals want the government to enforce 1920s republican laws such as bans on Islamic headwear and Moslem sects. The laws have been largely ignored in recent years.
The army briefly sent tanks onto the streets of an Islamist district of Ankara last month after anti-secularist protest there attended by the Iranian ambassador.
Newspapers on Monday quoted leading general Erol Ozkasnak as implicitly denying the military was working in close cooperation with Erbakan.

"The Turkish armed forces is in harmony with those who believe in the republic...and the implementation of its basic principles. It is not, and cannot be, in harmony with anyone else," the Sabah newspaper quoted Ozkasnak as saying.
Other papers carried the same statements, which Turkish political analysts said were a clear reference to the friction between the military and Erbakan's Islamists.
Erbakan faces an opposition censure motion in parliament on Tuesday. His coalition with free-marketeer Tansu Ciller has a majority of around six in the 550-seat assembly.
Istanbul shares fell 61 points, or 3.78 percent in afternoon trading on the politicial uncertrainty, brokers said.
"An easing in political tension is needed. Newspapers full of pictures of army generals negatively affect the market," said Mustafa Yilmaz who owns a brokerage.
